\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Encoded algebraic gate list]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.gatesBody}
\statementsource{Vad12}{
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p135-b001,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p135-b002
}
\label{Randomized.PIT.gatesBody}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.AlgGate, Randomized.AlgGate.encode}
Given a list of algebraic gates on $n$ variables, encode each gate and prefix its
encoding by the bit $1$, then concatenate these prefixed encodings in the original list
order.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Encoding a List of Algebraic Gates]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.encodeGates_eq}
\label{Randomized.PIT.encodeGates_eq}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.AlgCircuit.encodeGates, Randomized.AlgGate, Randomized.PIT.gatesBody}
\difficulty{4}
For any list $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ of algebraic gates, its encoding is the concatenation of
the marker bit $1$ followed by the encoding of each gate, in order, and a final marker
bit $0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Identity of the zero shift]
\lean{Randomized.AlgGate.shift_zero}
\label{Randomized.AlgGate.shift_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.AlgGate, Randomized.AlgGate.shift}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, shifting an algebraic gate by offset $0$ leaves it
unchanged; that is, the function sending each gate to its zero shift is the identity
function.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Shifted gate encoding]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.shiftGateW}
\label{Randomized.PIT.shiftGateW}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.PIT.arg1W, Randomized.PIT.arg2W, Randomized.PIT.isOneW, Randomized.PIT.isVarW, Randomized.PIT.tagBit}
Given Boolean lists $M$ and $w$, if $w$ encodes a variable, return the bit string $1000$
followed by its first argument encoding and then $0$. If $w$ encodes the constant $1$,
return $1001$. In every other case, return the bits $1$, the three tag bits of $w$, then
$M$, the first argument encoding, $0$, $M$, the second argument encoding, and $0$,
concatenated in that order.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Single shift step]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.shStep}
\label{Randomized.PIT.shStep}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Randomized.PIT.isDone, Randomized.PIT.restW, Randomized.PIT.sW, Randomized.PIT.shiftGateW, Turing.pairEncode}
For a Boolean list $D$, if the word extracted from its first component is done, return
$D$ unchanged. Otherwise, pair its first component with a pair consisting of the
remainder of that extracted word and the concatenation of the second component of the
inner pair with the shifted encoding of the extracted word.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Iterated shift run]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.shiftRun}
\label{Randomized.PIT.shiftRun}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Randomized.PIT.shStep, Turing.pairEncode}
For a Boolean list $z$, pair its first component with a pair of its second component and
the empty list, apply the single shift step $ (|z|+1)^1$ times, and return the second
component of the second component of the resulting list.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[One shift step on a nonempty gate list]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.shStep_cons}
\label{Randomized.PIT.shStep_cons}
\leanok
\uses{BoolCircuit.encodeNat, Complexity.BinArith.uHead_encodeNat, Complexity.BinArith.uRest_encodeNat, Complexity.isNilB, Randomized.AlgCircuit.encodeGates, Randomized.AlgGate, Randomized.AlgGate.encode, Randomized.AlgGate.shift, Randomized.PIT.arg1W, Randomized.PIT.arg2W, Randomized.PIT.bodyW, Randomized.PIT.isDone, Randomized.PIT.isOneW, Randomized.PIT.isVarW, Randomized.PIT.midW, Randomized.PIT.rest2W, Randomized.PIT.restW, Randomized.PIT.sW, Randomized.PIT.shStep, Randomized.PIT.shiftGateW, Randomized.PIT.tagBit, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n,m$ be natural numbers, let $g$ be an algebraic gate on $n$ variables, and let
$g_s$ be a finite list of such gates; let $o$ be any bit string. Applying one shift step
to the pairing of the unary string of length $m$ with the encoding of $g :: g_s$ paired
with $o$ yields the pairing of that same unary string with the encoding of $g_s$ paired
with $o$ followed by the bit $1$ and the encoding of $g$ with all node references
shifted by $m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed point of the empty circuit shift]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.shStep_nil}
\label{Randomized.PIT.shStep_nil}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.isNilB, Randomized.AlgCircuit.encodeGates, Randomized.AlgGate, Randomized.PIT.isDone, Randomized.PIT.sW, Randomized.PIT.shStep, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$ and all finite bit strings $M$ and $out$, one shift step
applied to the pairing of $M$ with the pairing of the encoding of the empty gate list
and $out$ leaves that bit string unchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Iteration of the gate-shifting step]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.iterate_shStep}
\label{Randomized.PIT.iterate_shStep}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.AlgCircuit.encodeGates, Randomized.AlgGate, Randomized.AlgGate.shift, Randomized.PIT.gatesBody, Randomized.PIT.shStep, Randomized.PIT.shStep_cons, Randomized.PIT.shStep_nil, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Fix an input width $n$ and a natural number $m$. For every finite list $gs$ of
arithmetic gates on $n$ inputs, output bit string $out$, and step count $T$ with
$|gs|\le T$, iterating the gate-shifting step $T$ times from the encoded state
containing the unary counter of length $m$, the encoded gates, and $out$ yields the
encoded state with that counter, the terminal marker, and $out$ followed by the
encodings of the gates in $gs$ after shifting each arithmetic reference by $m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Combined output length bound]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.length_uHead_add_uRest_le}
\label{Randomized.PIT.length_uHead_add_uRest_le}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.uHead, Complexity.BinArith.uRest}
\difficulty{4}
For every bit string $w$, run the two specified one-pass transducers on $w$: the first
outputs true bits while reading the initial run of true bits, and the second outputs the
suffix following the first false bit (or the empty word if there is no false bit). The
sum of the lengths of these two outputs is at most $|w|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[One shift step on a paired configuration]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.shStep_pair}
\label{Randomized.PIT.shStep_pair}

\uses{Complexity.pairFstD_pairEncode, Complexity.pairSndD_pairEncode, Randomized.PIT.arg1W, Randomized.PIT.arg2W, Randomized.PIT.bodyW, Randomized.PIT.length_uHead_add_uRest_le, Randomized.PIT.midW, Randomized.PIT.rest2W, Randomized.PIT.restW, Randomized.PIT.sW, Randomized.PIT.shStep, Randomized.PIT.shiftGateW, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}

\end{theorem}

\lean{Randomized.PIT.iterate_shStep_le}

\leanok
\uses{Randomized.PIT.shStep, Randomized.PIT.shStep_pair, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Fix an input width $n$. For any bit strings $M,w$ and any $i\in\mathbb{N}$, iterating
the gate-shifting step $i$ times from the encoded state containing $M$, $w$, and an
empty output produces bit strings $w'$ and $out'$ such that the resulting state encodes

\begin{definition}[Substitution witness encoding]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.subW}
\label{Randomized.PIT.subW}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.uHead, Complexity.BinArith.uRest, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Randomized.PIT.sI, Randomized.PIT.scanRun, Randomized.PIT.shiftRun, Turing.pairEncode}
For a Boolean list $x$, concatenate, in order: the head of the first component of its
first decoded pair; the bit $0$; the shift runs of the two encodings formed from the
empty list and the remainder of that first component, and from the scan encoding of that
component and the remainder of the second component; the bits $1011$; the scan encoding
of the first component with its first bit removed; the bit $0$; the concatenated scan
encodings of the first and second components with their first bit removed; and the bits
$00$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Encoding of a circuit difference]
\lean{Randomized.PIT.subW_eq}
\label{Randomized.PIT.subW_eq}
\leanok
\uses{BoolCircuit.encodeNat, Complexity.BinArith.uHead, Complexity.BinArith.uHead_encodeNat, Complexity.BinArith.uRest, Complexity.BinArith.uRest_encodeNat, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Randomized.AlgCircuit, Randomized.AlgCircuit.WellFormed, Randomized.AlgCircuit.decode, Randomized.AlgCircuit.encode, Randomized.AlgCircuit.encode_of_decode, Randomized.AlgCircuit.size, Randomized.AlgCircuit.subCircuit, Randomized.AlgGate.encode, Randomized.AlgGate.shift, Randomized.PIT.encodeGates_eq, Randomized.PIT.gatesBody, Randomized.PIT.sI, Randomized.PIT.sI_scanRun, Randomized.PIT.scanRun, Randomized.PIT.shiftRun, Randomized.PIT.shiftRun_eq, Randomized.PIT.subW, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Let $x$ be a finite bit string, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $C$ and $C'$ be
arithmetic circuits over $n$ input variables. Suppose the first and second components
parsed from $x$ decode, respectively, to the indexed circuits $(n,C)$ and $(n,C')$.
Assume each circuit is nonempty and every gate referring to earlier gates refers only to
gates with smaller indices. Then the string produced by the circuit-difference
construction on $x$ is the encoding of the circuit formed by appending the gates of
$C'$, with their references shifted by the size of $C$, to the gates of $C$, followed by
a subtraction gate whose inputs are the outputs of $C$ and the shifted copy of $C'$.
\end{theorem}

\lean{Randomized.polyTimeComputable_pitToZerop}
\label{Randomized.polyTimeComputable_pitToZerop}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_test_app, Complexity.BinArith.polyTimeComputable_uHead, Complexity.BinArith.uHead, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairFstD_pairEncode, Complexity.pairSndD, Complexity.pairSndD_pairEncode, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_and, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_const, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_ite, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_lenEq, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairSndD, Randomized.PIT.polyTimeComputable_subW, Randomized.PIT.polyTimeComputable_validW, Randomized.pitToZerop}

The following function on bit strings is polynomial-time computable: on input $x$,

assembled from the parsed circuits and their evaluations modulo the encoded prime, as
specified by the PIT transformation.

\uses{Randomized.PITLang, Randomized.ZEROP, Randomized.mem_PITLang_iff_pitToZerop, Randomized.pitToZerop, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_pitToZerop}
\difficulty{1}
The language of paired encodings of two well-formed algebraic circuits on the same
number of inputs whose associated integer polynomials are equal has a polynomial-time
many-one reduction to the language of encodings of well-formed algebraic circuits whose
associated integer polynomial is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Closure of coRP under reductions]
\lean{Randomized.coRP_PTM_of_polyTimeReducible}
\label{Randomized.coRP_PTM_of_polyTimeReducible}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.InCoRP.of_polyTimeReducible, Randomized.coRP_PTM, Randomized.mem_coRP_PTM_iff}
\difficulty{1}
Let $L$ and $L'$ be languages over the Boolean alphabet. If $L'$ is polynomial-time
many-one reducible to $L$ and $L$ belongs to coRP, then $L'$ belongs to coRP.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[One-Sided Randomized Membership]
\lean{Randomized.PITLang_mem_coRP_PTM_of_reduction}
\label{Randomized.PITLang_mem_coRP_PTM_of_reduction}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.PITLang, Randomized.PITLang_le_ZEROP, Randomized.ZEROP_mem_coRP_PTM, Randomized.coRP_PTM, Randomized.coRP_PTM_of_polyTimeReducible}
\difficulty{1}
The language of paired encodings of two well-formed algebraic circuits on the same
number of inputs whose associated integer polynomials are equal belongs to co-RP with
polynomial time bound, where acceptance is certain on inputs outside the language and
the probability of outputting true is at least $2/3$ on inputs in the language.
\end{theorem}
